title: Oil from gravel
hookLine: pressing gravel gives no oil, pressing sesame does: right practice bears fruit

cards: Some people swear by vision boards: picture it, want it badly enough, and it comes. Others say wanting is the problem, and you should stop hoping for anything.
Prince Jayasena, who doubted the novice yesterday, puts a version of this to a monk named Bhumija over a meal at his house.
Some teachers say, he tells Bhumija, that whether you hope for results or don't, you won't get them. What does your teacher say? Bhumija isn't sure.

teach.b: The Buddha's answer sets the hoping aside. The question isn't whether you wish. It's whether the method fits the goal.
Then four pictures, each a kitchen or farmyard job done wrong and done right. Someone who needs oil fills a tub with gravel, sprinkles it with water, and presses and presses.
Hope or no hope, no oil comes; gravel has none to give. Fill the tub with sesame and press: oil comes, whether you hoped or not. Someone who wants milk twists a cow's horn.
Nothing. Milk the udder: milk. Someone churns water hoping for butter.
Nothing. Churn curd: butter. Someone rubs a stick on wet, sappy wood to make fire.
Nothing. Use dry wood: fire. So too, the Buddha says, a seeker with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, on through the wrong path, gets no fruit, whether they hope or not.
Not because hoping is wrong, but because it's the wrong method. And anyone who practices the eightfold path rightly can reach the fruit, hoping or not.
Hope doesn't make gravel give oil, and indifference doesn't stop sesame from giving it.
In an ordinary week, that might mean: if a relationship needs listening, more hoping won't do it.
If your body needs sleep, wishing won't make up for it.
The Buddha's question is simple and a little blunt: what are you actually pressing?

how: Buddhist teachers use MN 126 to explain that the path depends on a fitting method rather than on wishing for results, setting the eightfold path, practiced rightly, against its wrong counterpart.

o: gravel, pressed again and again for nothing
a churn for turning curd into butter
sesame, the seed that gives oil when pressed

games.q: wrong tub, right tub: tap the pairs.

s: in MN 126 the Buddha says hoping for results is what blocks them
he sets hope aside: with the wrong method there's no fruit either way; with the right one there's fruit either way.
Bhumija asks the Buddha after a meal with Prince Jayasena
the prince put the question to him, and he brought it to the Buddha.
the eightfold path, practiced rightly, is the sesame in the simile
wrong view through wrong concentration is the gravel.

games.q: you need oil. you've filled the tub with gravel and you're hoping hard. what does the Buddha's simile say happens?
o: no oil comes, hope or no hope.
a little oil comes after a long time.
games.why: gravel has no oil to give. the problem is the method, not the wishing.

practice: Pick one thing you've been pushing at that isn't working, a habit, a conversation, a project, and ask quietly: am I pressing gravel, and what would sesame be here?
Let one small honest answer show up, then let it go and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Tila. Sesame, the seed that gives oil: pressing gravel never gives oil, however much you hope; pressing sesame does.

orig.note: Pali tila: sesame, the seed that gives oil in the Buddha's simile.

carryVoice: Your line: oil from sesame. What's in the tub matters more than the hoping. See you tomorrow.
